newsitem.title: USA: Small-company funds may offer bargains.
newsitem.headline: Small-company funds may offer bargains.

text.p: Many fund investors have given up looking for bargains in today's stock market. After all, the stock market's major indices have climbed by around 80 percent since 1995, setting a series of records.
But some analysts say there are plenty of bargains for investors who look in the right places. They cite small company stocks and the funds that hold them as a perfect example.

In fact, the gains in the stock market indices have been led by a small number of today's biggest, most popular firms. Stocks such as Intel (up 130.7 percent since 1995); IBM (up 96.4 percent); and Microsoft (up 88.3 percent) have accounted for the lion's share of the gains in the Dow Jones industrial average and the S&P 500.
Not surprisingly, funds that invest in large companies have gained an average of 25.8 percent since 1995, compared with a 20.7 percent annualized gain for the typical small-company growth fund.

But Chuck Carlson, editor of Dow Theory Forecasts, an investment newsletter in Hammond, Ind., figures small-company funds may soon start outperforming large-company funds. Among his reasons are that large companies' profits will slow this year.

Large companies, Carlson points out, have had much faster profit growth in recent quarters. That's due in large part to gains from overseas profits, and restructurings that have slashed the operating costs of many big firms.

But the strong U.S. dollar will reduce the value of profits that are counted in relatively weak overseas currencies. And many firms have done all they can to squeeze extra profits from their restructuring efforts.

The result is that the average profit gain for large companies will be only 15 percent in 1997, according to a consensus of analysts' estimates. That compares with a 35 percent estimated gain for the smaller companies that make up the Russell 200 Index.

Small stocks generally lead big stocks during the late stages of bull markets. The current bull market is looking long in the tooth. History suggests that we could see a small-cap stock rally before it ends.

Small stocks add diversification benefits. Small-company stocks tend to be more volatile than big-company shares, but the small fry actually can add a measure of safety to a portfolio that's heavily tilted toward blue chip stocks.
The reason is that shares of small and big companies often respond differently to factors such as interest rate fluctuations or other economic news.

"Many small companies are less affected by a slump in the economy," notes Carlson. "They can continue to grow their earnings when many large firms cannot." Small stocks perform better over long periods. Even if you're wrong in the short run, an investment in a small-company fund should help your portfolio's total return over time.

Since 1946, small-company shares have gained 13.9 percent annually vs. 12.2 percent for the S&P 500. That extra return compensates investors for the stocks' greater volatility -- and reflects small firms' ability to grow faster than more mature firms.
Carlson's final point: The small-cap sector includes some terrific funds.

His choices include Acorn Fund (800-922-6769; $1,000 minimum investment; no-load). Manager Robert Wanger and his team have led the fund to a 16.1 percent annualized return over the past five years vs. 12.8 percent for the average small-company growth fund. What's more, they've achieved those returns without making large bets on any one sector. For example, the fund's technology holdings recently accounted for only about 10 percent of the portfolio.

Another choice: PBHG Emerging Growth (800-433-0051; $2,500 minimum; no-load), the top-performing small-company growth fund during the three years through 1996, according to Lipper Analytical Services. Managers Gary Pilgrim and Christine Baxter use a computer model to find companies with the potential for positive earnings surprises.

For an indexed approach to small-cap investing, Dow Theory Forecasts recommends Vanguard Index Small-Cap Stock (800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum; no-load). The fund's 13.6 percent annualized return during the past five years beats the 13.1 percent annualized return of its index, the Russell 2000, during that time.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
